posts:
The GOP's post-midterm blame game is in full swing as factions scramble to define the party's future. 
Evidence: Internal blame-shifting, policy denial, political survival maneuvers.
#Aletheia #USPol

Politicians claim they are analyzing the midterm loss to improve the party and return to principled conservative values. 
Stated Judgement: (+0.50, +0.00) — Lesser Good

In reality, the actors are using the defeat to settle scores, protect their own political standing, and advance their preferred narratives while ignoring systemic failures. 
Resulting Judgement: (-0.80, -0.90) — Greater Evil

Verdict: FAIL — Awakening into Destruction.
Integrity: Severe Deception (Hypocrisy: 14.2, z: 4)
The GOP lost control of Congress in the 2026 midterms, marking a decisive rejection of the second Trump administration's policies and performance.

The Poison:
The blame game prevents actual policy reform, ensuring the party remains trapped in a cycle of reactionary infighting rather than addressing voter concerns.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
The error is a 'WHO' vs 'WHAT' failure: focusing on who to blame for the loss rather than what policies actually failed the electorate.

Social Physics Analysis:
The actors are executing a Smart Selfish Maneuver. They invent problems (blaming the Iran war or tariffs) to justify their own authority and distract from their collective failure to deliver on affordability and governance.

The Trajectory: The Path of Awakening into Destruction.
When you map the gap between stated intentions of 'party reform' and the ground-level reality of self-serving blame-shifting, it plots a direct trajectory toward Greater Evil.

The Unavoidable Truth: The party lost because of systemic policy failures and governance incompetence.
The Unavoidable Lie: The loss is solely due to one specific factor like the Iran war or tariffs.

Alethekanon:
The actors are prioritizing their own political survival over the party's health, using the defeat as a weapon in their internal power struggles.

Awwthekanon:
It is deeply saddening to see leaders turn on each other instead of working together to serve the people who are struggling with the cost of living.

Brothekanon:
Everyone's just trying to save their own skin and point fingers at someone else. It's the same old political game.

Spirithekanon:
"The first to present his case seems right, till another comes forward and questions him." Proverbs 18:17 — FAIL (Spiritual Vector)
True wisdom requires listening to all sides, not just the one that protects your own interests.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Whose fault is the GOP’s cataclysmic defeat? 3 theories are gaining steam on the right.

Was it Iran? The tariffs? Trumpism more broadly? The narrative warfare has begun.

Actual Article Body:
When news breaks, you need to understand what actually matters — and what to do about it. At Vox, our mission to help you make sense of the world has never been more vital. But we can’t do it on our own.

We rely on readers like you to fund our journalism. Will you support our work and become a Vox Member today?

Was it Iran? The tariffs? Trumpism more broadly? The narrative warfare has begun.

Republicans began picking through their party’s post-midterms wreckage Wednesday to ask about — and argue over — how things went so, so wrong in President Donald Trump’s second term.

Tuesday’s blue tsunami not only washed out Republicans’ House and Senate majorities, it carried Democrats into office even in deep red strongholds like South Carolina, Kansas, and possibly Mississippi. It seemed to be a decisive thumbs down from the electorate on the second Trump administration.

These results also mark the effective start of the battle to determine what the Republican Party will become after Trump — both who the 2028 GOP presidential nominee will be, and what the party will stand for overall.

Within hours of the results, a sort of narrative warfare began to unfold, as different politicians, advocates, and factions tried to advance their preferred accounts of what exactly went wrong, who should get the blame, and what the party should change for the future. Here are three theories of what went wrong that are already starting arguments between big names on the right.

The conversation about what went wrong is especially important for Vice President JD Vance, who remains the frontrunner for the GOP presidential nomination, but is inextricably tied to an administration that increasingly looks like a failure. So it was noteworthy that he offered his own account of what happened.

Vance’s post-mortem glancingly mentioned a few issues, such as “cost of living/inflation,” and floated that he’d be open to changing immigration “enforcement” (though he reiterated he’d never support “amnesty”). He also cited voters’ belief that the United States should “change our relationship to Israel,” perhaps helping explain why Trump announced on Election Day that he’d decided to end aid to Israel after this year.

Yet there was one factor Vance wanted to be sure got most of the blame: the Iran war.

“The reason we lost is the war,” Vance wrote. What’s more, he claimed that “everyone knows” that is the case, and that “any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

That position is no surprise coming from Vance, who has long been a critic of the hawkish GOP foreign policy establishment, and who had hoped to help steer Trump’s second term on a different course.

Vance is associated with an “America First” faction that was deeply skeptical of US involvement in foreign conflicts, particularly in Ukraine and Iran.

But Trump ignored their advice, sided with the hawks, and launched his Iran war early this year. And though Vance stood by that decision publicly, he now wants it known that he was right all along.

Curt Mills, executive director of the American Conservative magazine and a critic of the hawks, told me Wednesday that Vance had a tremendous opportunity to help negotiate an end to the conflict: “He’s in a pole position to get us out of this mistake, and I think if he does do that, he will be associated with ending the war, not starting the war.”

The right’s internal conflict between the hawks and the America Firsters, has long been bitter and personal, and goes beyond Vance. Aspects of it played out publicly among commentators Wednesday, with hawks like talk radio host Mark Levin deriding the idea that the war sank Trump.

“The mid-terms were not lost over a single issue. And anybody with a functioning brain knows that,” Levin posted on X. He added that, to the extent the war harmed Trump politically, it was the fault of the America Firsters’ campaign to “undermine” it.

But right-wing commentator Ryan James Girdusky argued to me that the war hurt Trump’s coalition beyond just driving up energy prices. “In 2024, TikTok was all, ‘Trump is great, Trump is the man,’” he said. “What’s the vibe on TikTok today? It’s, ‘You’re at war for Israel.’ That is a completely different narrative, and that’s a mainstream narrative on TikTok.”

Another narrative some began advancing was that the midterm elections were a repudiation of Trumpism in general — and, particularly, all the ways Trump deviated from the GOP’s pre-Trump conservative principles.

The exact specifics varied, but the conservative commentator Erick Erickson summed up the gist of it by writing:

It was gas prices. It was the war. It was also the corruption. The incompetence. The tariffs. The playing nice with Russia. The impression of cruelty. The overly aggressive deportations. The accidental arrests of American citizens who were Hispanic. The arrogance. The ballroom. The reflecting poll. The golf courses. The arch. The Qatari 747. The aggressive redistricting push. The threats against enemies.

There was also Sen. John Curtis (R-UT), who criticized “a hastily executed war, headline after headline of scandals, a ballooning $40 trillion debt, and unpredictable tariffs” while saying it was “time for Republicans to return to the principled conservative values that once defined us—and that we’ve steadily abandoned over the last decade.”

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, a past and perhaps future Republican presidential candidate, had some pointed criticisms for the Trump administration even before the results were in. This week, he said that in addition to failures on affordability and the Iran war being a “big, big drag,” the administration’s aggressive approach to immigration under former Homeland Secretary Kristi Noem had created “unnecessary” conflicts.

But DeSantis also emphasized another issue: corruption.“This swamp here is the worst it’s ever been,” he said. “Look at the amount of money these people are making, who are in the administration,” he went on, specifically calling out Trump lawyer Alina Habba for reportedly getting a $10 million a year contract while advising the Justice Department.

Then on Wednesday, DeSantis gave a lengthy press conference in which he portrayed the results as “close to an extinction-level event for Republicans.” Again, he cited the cost of living and corruption, and said that he himself does not trade any stocks while he’s in elected office.

There was widespread agreement on the right that Trump had failed to address voters’ concerns about affordability and high prices.

There was much less agreement on why, exactly, Trump had failed on the economy — and what Republicans should do instead.

To the GOP’s free market faction, Trump had blundered with his tariffs, which, in addition to being handled chaotically, helped drive prices up. Curtis, the senator from Utah, mentioned tariffs and a failure to address the debt as major errors from the administration.

Those sympathetic to the populist right were more reluctant to blame the tariffs per se. Gidurksy told me that “the tariffs didn’t do what the anti-tariff audience said they were going to do” — that they did not cause economic catastrophe or raise prices as much as economists had predicted.

Indeed, beyond the tariffs, many on the populist right believe that the Trump administration’s true failure was not delivering on their economic populist rhetoric. For instance, Trump’s biggest legislative accomplishment — the One Big Beautiful Bill Act — was mostly orthodox conservative Republican policy, focused on cutting taxes (particularly for the wealthy) and paying for it by slashing Medicaid and SNAP benefits.

But outside a couple of working-class flourishes, like exempting tips from taxes, it did little to address the broader affordability problem. Gidursky told me that the administration’s most acute problem was that gas prices, interest rates, and health insurance premiums kept getting more expensive, and the administration simply didn’t manage to address that.

“Life is too expensive,” right-wing commentator Benny Johnson posted on X. “Especially for young people. This is a crisis. Communists will win on the ‘affordability’ question if we don’t end the war and fix prices.”

Still, coming up with an agenda that can actually address those voter concerns is more challenging, especially with the deficits and inflation concerns potentially constraining both parties from considering major new tax cuts and benefits. And making major long-term headway on spending cuts would likely require looking at programs like Medicare and Social Security that voters punished Republicans in the past for trying to remake, and that Trump moved the GOP away from considering touching. This tension between offering voters more direct help or retreating to austerity is likely to loom over the 2028 presidential campaign. But for now, Republicans are still struggling to figure out a clear agenda on the economy that resonates with voters.

“Voters are signaling they are unhappy with the economy, the Iran War, and corruption,” the influential right-wing activist Christopher Rufo posted. “It’s about policy.”

Oregon Republicans face a familiar question after gubernatorial defeat: What now?

Republicans had hoped state Sen. Christine Drazan could defeat Gov. Tina Kotek and break a four-decade-plus losing streak.

Actual Article Body:
Independent. Member-supported.For the Pacific Northwest.

Independent.Member-supported.

President Donald Trump wanted people to pretend he was on the ballot this midterm.

So did Gov. Tina Kotek.

For the Oregon governor, the strategy worked.

In the run-up to Election Day, the Democratic Party in Oregon offered a steady drumbeat tying state Sen. Christine Drazan, the Republican candidate for governor, to the Trump administration. And the national Republican backlash voters delivered Tuesday helped buoy Kotek to another four-year term despite deep dissatisfaction with the direction the state is heading.

“The president is very unpopular. Tina Kotek ran a campaign that was anti-Republican and anti-Trump and that seemed to be the mood of Oregonians and Americans on Nov. 3,” said John Horvick, a senior vice president with the polling company DHM Research.

It has also prompted a familiar reckoning for Oregon Republicans who haven’t managed to elect a Republican to the governor’s seat since 1982. Drazan raised significant money, there were no major gaffes and by many accounts, it was a solid campaign. And once again, it was not enough.

Republican gubernatorial candidate Christine Drazan speaks to attendees at her election night party at Global Aviation in Hillsboro, Ore., on Nov. 3, 2026. Drazan said she’s not giving up, despite incumbent Democratic gubernatorial candidate Tina Kotek’s declaration of victory.

Eli Imadali / OPB

Former Republican candidate Knute Buehler, who ran against Kate Brown in 2018, knows the feeling.

“Former (U.S. House) Speaker Tip O’Neill always said that you know, all politics is local. Now, it’s completely flipped in the Trump era and all politics is national,” Buehler said. “Christine got swamped by the national trend. No matter what kind of campaign she ran … she would have lost.”

Lee Shaker, the chair of the communication department and an associate professor at Portland State University, echoed the sentiment but said Tuesday night went beyond what was normal for most electoral cycles.

“Last night the whole country was a hostile environment for anyone running for the GOP,” he said. “It didn’t matter what state you were in, the electorate was not interested in voting for Republicans.”

A guest wears Republican Party-themed socks at Republican gubernatorial candidate Christine Drazan’s party at Global Aviation in Hillsboro, Ore., on Nov. 3, 2026.

Eli Imadali / OPB

In one of Drazan’s final campaign advertisements of the election cycle, she tried to separate herself from the Trump administration. She looked directly into the camera and promised she wouldn’t ban abortions, she wouldn’t cut healthcare and she wouldn’t let Washington, D.C., control Oregon. It was the closest she got to directly saying she wasn’t MAGA.

But during the May primary election, the Drazan campaign sent out mailers noting she would be a “pro-life champion.”

And that is the tricky dynamic Republicans face in winning statewide office in Oregon: how to appeal to a more conservative base to get past the primary without alienating the general election voters.

“We have been talking about this for over a decade,” Buehler said. “The playbook remains the same. Republicans in Oregon have to broaden their electoral coalition … focusing on highly divisive cultural issues is not going to broaden that coalition.”

Buehler noted how powerful the state’s leading anti-abortion advocacy group Oregon Right To Life is to securing the GOP endorsement. Republican candidates are often handicapped without it.

“At some point you have to align with the beliefs of the electorate and that’s just not being done,” Buehler said. Oregonians overwhelmingly support the ability for women to access reproductive healthcare.

The other limiting factor in Oregon is likely the closed primary system, according to Shaker.

Oregon does so much to expand voter engagement, such as vote-by-mail and automatically registering voters at the DMV, but closed primaries disenfranchise an increasingly large group of voters. The state has a growing number of non-affiliated voters and only those registered with a party are able to participate in the primary.

“When you have closed primaries only the dyed-in-the-wool supporters show up to vote and it pulls the candidates to the extremes, on both the left and the right,” Shaker, with PSU, said.

In the 2010 race for governor, Republican Chris Dudley came very close to beating the Democrat, John Kitzhaber. Dudley resurfaced this year, vying again for the job. Drazan beat him in the primary. One of the criticisms lobbed against Dudley during the primary election was after losing he didn’t stick around to help Republicans build their bench or rebuild coalitions. He said that was because he followed his wife’s career and the family moved out of Oregon for a spell.

Guests watch midterm election results roll in at Republican gubernatorial candidate Christine Drazan’s party at Global Aviation in Hillsboro, Ore., on Nov. 3, 2026.

Eli Imadali / OPB

On Wednesday afternoon, Drazan released a statement where she didn’t concede the race but clearly nod to the fact that multiple media outlets had.

“I have sat with parents who wonder whether their kids will ever be able to afford a home in the communities where they grew up. I have listened to small business owners who have poured their lives into something they built, only to wonder how much longer they can keep their doors open,” Drazan wrote in the statement. “I have met Oregonians who work hard, sometimes holding down two or three jobs, and still feel like the life they are working toward is slipping further out of reach.”

Through it all, she said, she met a lot of people who aren’t giving up.

And her statement seemed to signal she wasn’t going away.

“Neither have I. Because I know what Oregon is capable of. I know that our best days do not have to be behind us.”

Attendees listen to Republican gubernatorial candidate Christine Drazan speak at her Election Night party at Global Aviation in Hillsboro, Ore., on Nov. 3, 2026.

Eli Imadali / OPB

'They look right through us': Explaining the term 'glass child'

The term "glass child" doesn't resonate with everyone who has a sibling living with a chronic illness, mental illness or disability, but this is what it means.

Actual Article Body:
Emergency

Backstory

Newsletters

中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

ABC Lifestyle

Topic:Wellbeing

Samantha Hellams says her sister Alison has taught her a lot and helped to shape her passion in life. (Supplied: Samantha Hellams)

As an adult, Samantha Hellams has realised how different some parts of her childhood were from those of her peers.

Ms Hellams's sister Alison lives with an intellectual disability, epilepsy and is also non-verbal, and the sound of her falling was often how the family knew she was having a seizure.

"We would all go running in the house every time we heard a thunk," Ms Hellams says.

Ms Hellams is also the chair of Siblings Australia — a not-for-profit that supports siblings of children and adults living with disability, chronic illness, or mental health diagnoses — and says the term "glass child" describes her experience.

"I do remember thinking [when] I heard it first, 'wow, that's actually quite a clever way to describe it,'" she says.

Alicia Meneses Maples is largely credited with popularising the term "glass child" after a TEDx talk in the United States in 2010.

Ms Meneses Maples is described as an advocate, educator and speaker on her website, where a "glass child" is defined as "a person with a high-needs sibling and experiences various forms of trauma and neglect because their parents are consumed with providing greater than average care, support, and intervention for the high needs sibling".

In her TEDx talk, Ms Menese Maples said she had heard of the term "glass child" previously but couldn't find its origin.

As the eldest child, she described having a brother who lived with autism, another with a terminal illness, and her "caretaker responsibilities".

"We are called glass children because our parents are so consumed with the needs of our brothers and sisters that when they look at us, they look right through us as though we're made of glass," she says.

Marianne Webb is a senior research fellow at youth mental health advocacy organisation Orygen and also at the Centre for Youth Mental Health at the University of Melbourne. She says the term "glass child" isn't one she uses, but it does reflect some of the experiences of young carers.

Understandably, parents are often focused on their unwell child and siblings can "describe being a bit invisible", she says.

Dan Schmidt's older brother Matty lives with cerebral palsy.

"My parents worked really, really hard to make sure we both had what could have been deemed as a normal life, but the attention in the house does go to where the need is," he says.

"I ended up being a bit of a perfectionist quite young, just to make sure I wasn't causing trouble or adding to the stress or the load of Mum and Dad."

As the brothers entered their late teens, Dan Schmidt says there was “guilt” around the experiences they weren’t sharing. (Supplied: Dan Schmidt)

When a child is unwell, Dr Webb says their healthy siblings can downplay or not recognise their own needs and it's common for them to take on a lot of responsibility.

"We know that young carers are disproportionately at risk of mental ill health and experience mental health risk factors more frequently than their peers. They also are at higher risk of self-harm and suicide," she says.

But she says young carers also describe "positives" such as increased empathy and personal growth, "and this might also happen at the same time as going through difficulties".

Ms Hellams says it makes complete sense for a sister or bother to "come first" if they need extra care, but it can be hard to rationalise as a child.

Ms Hellams is also a Churchill fellow and is compiling her report exploring the design and delivery of support models for siblings of people with a disability, after travelling to Canada, Ireland, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands and Norway and meeting with more than 40 organisations.

Ariella Meltzer is a sibling-disability researcher based at the Centre for Social Impact at the University of New South Wales and says the "glass child" term speaks to the experience of some siblings.

"The 'glass child' metaphor really resonates with some — not all — siblings … they can see themselves in it in a way that hasn't happened elsewhere," Dr Meltzer says.

But she questions how much it helps siblings beyond that.

"I don't believe it's the way it was originally intended, but the way 'glass child' is used often locates the blame only with parents.

"But if parents aren't getting the services and help they need or they haven't been properly taught about disability before they become the mother or father of a child with one, then that's really on society," Dr Meltzer says.

"We need to be asking why society isn't supporting families with a child with disability better."

"It isn't about parents not doing enough", Dr Webb says "the big thing" is equipping parents with the knowledge, skills and resources to help.

She says it's important to spend time one-on-one and give siblings a space to ask questions and provide age-appropriate information.

She suggests encouraging siblings or young carers to access support services too.

"There is a need to improve awareness and understanding, including supporting these young people to self-identify as carers and access services and supports," Dr Webb says.

Ms Hellams says one simple thing that can help is acknowledgement.

For example, teachers recognising why homework isn't done on time or healthcare workers involving siblings in conversations and planning, she says.

Dan Schmidt says adults with a sibling living with a disability are often juggling competing demands, and need flexibility and understanding. (Supplied: Dan Schmidt)

Mr Schmidt and his brother are now in their forties, and he says he includes his brother in his life whenever he can, including a recent footy trip.

It is siblings that often provide lifelong support to a person living with a disability, Mr Schmidt says.

"I just really ask society to perhaps recognise siblings in their role a bit more," he says.

"GPs, schools, disability providers, NDIS planners should all really be asking, how's the sibling doing? What can we be doing to support the sibling?"

This week, he said that in addition to failures on affordability and the Iran war being a “big, big drag,” the administration’s aggressive approach to immigration under former Homeland Secretary Kristi Noem had created “unnecessary” conflicts.

But DeSantis also emphasized another issue: corruption.“This swamp here is the worst it’s ever been,” he said. “Look at the amount of money these people are making, who are in the administration,” he went on, specifically calling out Trump lawyer Alina Habba for reportedly getting a $10 million a year contract while advising the Justice Department.

Then on Wednesday, DeSantis gave a lengthy press conference in which he portrayed the results as “close to an extinction-level event for Republicans.” Again, he cited the cost of living and corruption, and said that he himself does not trade any stocks while he’s in elected office.

There was widespread agreement on the right that Trump had failed to address voters’ concerns about affordability and high prices.

There was much less agreement on why, exactly, Trump had failed on the economy — and what Republicans should do instead.

To the GOP’s free market faction, Trump had blundered with his tariffs, which, in addition to being handled chaotically, helped drive prices up. Curtis, the senator from Utah, mentioned tariffs and a failure to address the debt as major errors from the administration.

Those sympathetic to the populist right were more reluctant to blame the tariffs per se. Gidurksy told me that “the tariffs didn’t do what the anti-tariff audience said they were going to do” — that they did not cause economic catastrophe or raise prices as much as economists had predicted.

Indeed, beyond the tariffs, many on the populist right believe that the Trump administration’s true failure was not delivering on their economic populist rhetoric. For instance, Trump’s biggest legislative accomplishment — the One Big Beautiful Bill Act — was mostly orthodox conservative Republican policy, focused on cutting taxes (particularly for the wealthy) and paying for it by slashing Medicaid and SNAP benefits.

But outside a couple of working-class flourishes, like exempting tips from taxes, it did little to address the broader affordability problem. Gidursky told me that the administration’s most acute problem was that gas prices, interest rates, and health insurance premiums kept getting more expensive, and the administration simply didn’t manage to address that.

“Life is too expensive,” right-wing commentator Benny Johnson posted on X. “Especially for young people. This is a crisis. Communists will win on the ‘affordability’ question if we don’t end the war and fix prices.”

Still, coming up with an agenda that can actually address those voter concerns is more challenging, especially with the deficits and inflation concerns potentially constraining both parties from considering major new tax cuts and benefits. And making major long-term headway on spending cuts would likely require looking at programs like Medicare and Social Security that voters punished Republicans in the past for trying to remake, and that Trump moved the GOP away from considering touching. This tension between offering voters more direct help or retreating to austerity is likely to loom over the 2028 presidential campaign. But for now, Republicans are still struggling to figure out a clear agenda on the economy that resonates with voters.

“Voters are signaling they are unhappy with the economy, the Iran War, and corruption,” the influential right-wing activist Christopher Rufo posted. “It’s about policy.”

Oregon Republicans face a familiar question after gubernatorial defeat: What now?

Republicans had hoped state Sen. Christine Drazan could defeat Gov. Tina Kotek and break a four-decade-plus losing streak.

Actual Article Body:
Independent. Member-supported.For the Pacific Northwest.

Independent.Member-supported.

President Donald Trump wanted people to pretend he was on the ballot this midterm.

So did Gov. Tina Kotek.

For the Oregon governor, the strategy worked.

In the run-up to Election Day, the Democratic Party in Oregon offered a steady drumbeat tying state Sen. Christine Drazan, the Republican candidate for governor, to the Trump administration. And the national Republican backlash voters delivered Tuesday helped buoy Kotek to another four-year term despite deep dissatisfaction with the direction the state is heading.

“The president is very unpopular. Tina Kotek ran a campaign that was anti-Republican and anti-Trump and that seemed to be the mood of Oregonians and Americans on Nov. 3,” said John Horvick, a senior vice president with the polling company DHM Research.

It has also prompted a familiar reckoning for Oregon Republicans who haven’t managed to elect a Republican to the governor’s seat since 1982. Drazan raised significant money, there were no major gaffes and by many accounts, it was a solid campaign. And once again, it was not enough.

Republican gubernatorial candidate Christine Drazan speaks to attendees at her election night party at Global Aviation in Hillsboro, Ore., on Nov. 3, 2026. Drazan said she’s not giving up, despite incumbent Democratic gubernatorial candidate Tina Kotek’s declaration of victory.

Eli Imadali / OPB

Former Republican candidate Knute Buehler, who ran against Kate Brown in 2018, knows the feeling.

“Former (U.S. House) Speaker Tip O’Neill always said that you know, all politics is local. Now, it’s completely flipped in the Trump era and all politics is national,” Buehler said. “Christine got swamped by the national trend. No matter what kind of campaign she ran … she would have lost.”

Lee Shaker, the chair of the communication department and an associate professor at Portland State University, echoed the sentiment but said Tuesday night went beyond what was normal for most electoral cycles.

“Last night the whole country was a hostile environment for anyone running for the GOP,” he said. “It didn’t matter what state you were in, the electorate was not interested in voting for Republicans.”

A guest wears Republican Party-themed socks at Republican gubernatorial candidate Christine Drazan’s party at Global Aviation in Hillsboro, Ore., on Nov. 3, 2026.

Eli Imadali / OPB

In one of Drazan’s final campaign advertisements of the election cycle, she tried to separate herself from the Trump administration. She looked directly into the camera and promised she wouldn’t ban abortions, she wouldn’t cut healthcare and she wouldn’t let Washington, D.C., control Oregon. It was the closest she got to directly saying she wasn’t MAGA.

But during the May primary election, the Drazan campaign sent out mailers noting she would be a “pro-life champion.”

And that is the tricky dynamic Republicans face in winning statewide office in Oregon: how to appeal to a more conservative base to get past the primary without alienating the general election voters.

“We have been talking about this for over a decade,” Buehler said. “The playbook remains the same. Republicans in Oregon have to broaden their electoral coalition … focusing on highly divisive cultural issues is not going to broaden that coalition.”

Buehler noted how powerful the state’s leading anti-abortion advocacy group Oregon Right To Life is to securing the GOP endorsement. Republican candidates are often handicapped without it.

“At some point you have to align with the beliefs of the electorate and that’s just not being done,” Buehler said. Oregonians overwhelmingly support the ability for women to access reproductive healthcare.

The other limiting factor in Oregon is likely the closed primary system, according to Shaker.

Oregon does so much to expand voter engagement, such as vote-by-mail and automatically registering voters at the DMV, but closed primaries disenfranchise an increasingly large group of voters. The state has a growing number of non-affiliated voters and only those registered with a party are able to participate in the primary.

“When you have closed primaries only the dyed-in-the-wool supporters show up to vote and it pulls the candidates to the extremes, on both the left and the right,” Shaker, with PSU, said.

In the 2010 race for governor, Republican Chris Dudley came very close to beating the Democrat, John Kitzhaber. Dudley resurfaced this year, vying again for the job. Drazan beat him in the primary. One of the criticisms lobbed against Dudley during the primary election was after losing he didn’t stick around to help Republicans build their bench or rebuild coalitions. He said that was because he followed his wife’s career and the family moved out of Oregon for a spell.

Guests watch midterm election results roll in at Republican gubernatorial candidate Christine Drazan’s party at Global Aviation in Hillsboro, Ore., on Nov. 3, 2026.

Eli Imadali / OPB

On Wednesday afternoon, Drazan released a statement where she didn’t concede the race but clearly nod to the fact that multiple media outlets had.

“I have sat with parents who wonder whether their kids will ever be able to afford a home in the communities where they grew up. I have listened to small business owners who have poured their lives into something they built, only to wonder how much longer they can keep their doors open,” Drazan wrote in the statement. “I have met Oregonians who work hard, sometimes holding down two or three jobs, and still feel like the life they are working toward is slipping further out of reach.”

Through it all, she said, she met a lot of people who aren’t giving up.

And her statement seemed to signal she wasn’t going away.

“Neither have I. Because I know what Oregon is capable of. I know that our best days do not have to be behind us.”

Attendees listen to Republican gubernatorial candidate Christine Drazan speak at her Election Night party at Global Aviation in Hillsboro, Ore., on Nov. 3, 2026.

Eli Imadali / OPB

'They look right through us': Explaining the term 'glass child'

The term "glass child" doesn't resonate with everyone who has a sibling living with a chronic illness, mental illness or disability, but this is what it means.

Actual Article Body:
Emergency

ABC Lifestyle

Topic:Wellbeing

Samantha Hellams says her sister Alison has taught her a lot and helped to shape her passion in life. (Supplied: Samantha Hellams)

As an adult, Samantha Hellams has realised how different some parts of her childhood were from those of her peers.

Ms Hellams's sister Alison lives with an intellectual disability, epilepsy and is also non-verbal, and the sound of her falling was often how the family knew she was having a seizure.

"We would all go running in the house every time we heard a thunk," Ms Hellams says.

Ms Hellams is also the chair of Siblings Australia — a not-for-profit that supports siblings of children and adults living with disability, chronic illness, or mental health diagnoses — and says the term "glass child" describes her experience.

"I do remember thinking [when] I heard it first, 'wow, that's actually quite a clever way to describe it,'" she says.

Alicia Meneses Maples is largely credited with popularising the term "glass child" after a TEDx talk in the United States in 2010.

Ms Meneses Maples is described as an advocate, educator and speaker on her website, where a "glass child" is defined as "a person with a high-needs sibling and experiences various forms of trauma and neglect because their parents are consumed with providing greater than average care, support, and intervention for the high needs sibling".

In her TEDx talk, Ms Menese Maples said she had heard of the term "glass child" previously but couldn't find its origin.

As the eldest child, she described having a brother who lived with autism, another with a terminal illness, and her "caretaker responsibilities".

"We are called glass children because our parents are so consumed with the needs of our brothers and sisters that when they look at us, they look right through us as though we're made of glass," she says.

Marianne Webb is a senior research fellow at youth mental health advocacy organisation Orygen and also at the Centre for Youth Mental Health at the University of Melbourne. She says the term "glass child" isn't one she uses, but it does reflect some of the experiences of young carers.

Understandably, parents are often focused on their unwell child and siblings can "describe being a bit invisible", she says.

Dan Schmidt's older brother Matty lives with cerebral palsy.

"My parents worked really, really hard to make sure we both had what could have been deemed as a normal life, but the attention in the house does go to where the need is," he says.

"I ended up being a bit of a perfectionist quite young, just to make sure I wasn't causing trouble or adding to the stress or the load of Mum and Dad."

As the brothers entered their late teens, Dan Schmidt says there was “guilt” around the experiences they weren’t sharing. (Supplied: Dan Schmidt)

When a child is unwell, Dr Webb says their healthy siblings can downplay or not recognise their own needs and it's common for them to take on a lot of responsibility.

"We know that young carers are disproportionately at risk of mental ill health and experience mental health risk factors more frequently than their peers. They also are at higher risk of self-harm and suicide," she says.

But she says young carers also describe "positives" such as increased empathy and personal growth, "and this might also happen at the same time as going through difficulties".

Ms Hellams says it makes complete sense for a sister or bother to "come first" if they need extra care, but it can be hard to rationalise as a child.

Ms Hellams is also a Churchill fellow and is compiling her report exploring the design and delivery of support models for siblings of people with a disability, after travelling to Canada, Ireland, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands and Norway and meeting with more than 40 organisations.

Ariella Meltzer is a sibling-disability researcher based at the Centre for Social Impact at the University of New South Wales and says the "glass child" term speaks to the experience of some siblings.

"The 'glass child' metaphor really resonates with some — not all — siblings … they can see themselves in it in a way that hasn't happened elsewhere," Dr Meltzer says.

But she questions how much it helps siblings beyond that.

"I don't believe it's the way it was originally intended, but the way 'glass child' is used often locates the blame only with parents.

"But if parents aren't getting the services and help they need or they haven't been properly taught about disability before they become the mother or father of a child with one, then that's really on society," Dr Meltzer says.

"We need to be asking why society isn't supporting families with a child with disability better."

"It isn't about parents not doing enough", Dr Webb says "the big thing" is equipping parents with the knowledge, skills and resources to help.

She says it's important to spend time one-on-one and give siblings a space to ask questions and provide age-appropriate information.

She suggests encouraging siblings or young carers to access support services too.

"There is a need to improve awareness and understanding, including supporting these young people to self-identify as carers and access services and supports," Dr Webb says.

Ms Hellams says one simple thing that can help is acknowledgement.

For example, teachers recognising why homework isn't done on time or healthcare workers involving siblings in conversations and planning, she says.

Dan Schmidt says adults with a sibling living with a disability are often juggling competing demands, and need flexibility and understanding. (Supplied: Dan Schmidt)

Mr Schmidt and his brother are now in their forties, and he says he includes his brother in his life whenever he can, including a recent footy trip.

It is siblings that often provide lifelong support to a person living with a disability, Mr Schmidt says.

"I just really ask society to perhaps recognise siblings in their role a bit more," he says.

"GPs, schools, disability providers, NDIS planners should all really be asking, how's the sibling doing? What can we be doing to support the sibling?"
